strengths: Well-motivated problem setting: Aligning frozen unimodal vision and language representations using only limited paired data and abundant unpaired data addresses a significant real-world bottleneck where multimodal paired datasets are expensive or scarce.

Elegant and practical theoretical contribution: Theorem 5.1 / C.4 provides an explicit, closed-form gradient for the KLOT divergence via the envelope theorem. This cleanly avoids both memory-heavy Sinkhorn unrolling and computationally expensive implicit differentiation, allowing large batch training (up to 32k) on a single GPU.

Comprehensive and convincing empirical validation: SOTAlign consistently outperforms supervised baselines (SAIL) and semi-supervised approaches (STRUCTURE, NNCLR, S-CLIP, SUE) across zero-shot retrieval (COCO, Flickr30k) and classification benchmarks (ImageNet, CIFAR, DTD, Food-101).

Insightful analysis of distribution shift: The authors quantify the domain discrepancy between paired and unpaired data using Spherical Sliced Wasserstein (SSW) distance, demonstrating a strong negative correlation between SSW distance and downstream performance gains.
weaknesses: Minor mathematical typo in the main text: In Theorem 5.1 (Equation 13 on page 5), the denominator is written as $\epsilon^*$, whereas the derivation in Appendix Theorem C.4 correctly yields $\epsilon$ (the entropic parameter associated with the predicted affinity matrix $K$). The authors should fix this typo in Equation 13.

Architectural expressivity: Appendix A.1 notes that the alignment layers $f$ and $g$ are restricted to linear projections because non-linear layers were less robust under low supervision. While understandable, this means both the teacher and student models are effectively linear mappings on top of frozen representations; further analysis or discussion on why non-linear layers underperform and whether regularizations could mitigate this would strengthen the work.

Ablation on batch size sensitivity: SOTAlign relies on large batch sizes (up to 32k) to compute batch-level optimal transport plans. It is not fully explored how sensitive the method is to significantly smaller mini-batch sizes (e.g., 256 or 1024), which is relevant for environments with more constrained hardware.

strengths: Practical and well-motivated setting: Addressing vision-language alignment under scarce paired supervision by leveraging frozen unimodal encoders and unpaired data is a timely, impactful research direction that directly connects to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.

Theoretical and computational contribution: Deriving the closed-form gradient for the entropic optimal transport divergence (Theorem 5.1 / C.4) via the envelope theorem eliminates the severe memory explosion of unrolled Sinkhorn iterations and the runtime overhead of implicit differentiation, enabling scaling to large batch sizes (up to 32k).

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation: The paper benchmarks against a wide spectrum of baselines (supervised SAIL, STRUCTURE, NNCLR, S-CLIP, SUE) across both zero-shot retrieval (COCO, Flickr30k) and diverse zero-shot classification benchmarks (ImageNet, Food-101, CIFAR-10/100, DTD, etc.), showing consistent, notable gains.

Thorough analytical insights: The paper provides informative ablations and scaling studies, including the effect of supervision regimes, volume of unpaired samples, encoder compatibility (mutual k-NN), and an insightful quantitative analysis of cross-domain distribution shifts using Spherical Sliced Wasserstein (SSW) distances.
weaknesses: Notation typo in Theorem 5.1: In Equation (13) of the main text, the denominator is written as $\epsilon^*$, whereas the actual derivative with respect to $K$ (as correctly shown in Theorem C.4, Equation 28) has $\epsilon$ in the denominator. This typo should be corrected to avoid confusion.

Hardware demands and batch-size sensitivity: The framework relies on large batch sizes (up to 32k, composed of 10k pairs and unpaired samples) to compute representative mini-batch transport plans on an 80GB A100. The paper would benefit from explicitly analyzing sensitivity and performance degradation under hardware-constrained smaller batch sizes (e.g., 256, 512, 1024).

Throughput and wall-clock overhead analysis: While Figure 6 benchmarks memory and execution time for the gradient computation in isolation, there is limited reporting of total end-to-end training runtime and computational throughput comparison against standard contrastive learning (SAIL) across the 2,000 training iterations.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: aligning unimodal pretrained models under severely limited supervision using abundant unpaired data, providing empirical validation for the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.

Derives an explicit closed-form gradient for the KL divergence between entropic optimal transport plans (Theorem 5.1 and Theorem C.4), eliminating the need for memory-intensive Sinkhorn unrolling or computationally expensive implicit differentiation and enabling scaling to large batch sizes.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across diverse tasks (zero-shot retrieval on COCO/Flickr30k and zero-shot classification on ImageNet and fine-grained datasets), demonstrating substantial and consistent improvements over strong supervised (SAIL) and semi-supervised (STRUCTURE, S-CLIP, NNCLR, SUE) baselines.

Insightful analysis of data distribution shifts, showing a strong negative correlation between Spherical Sliced Wasserstein (SSW) distance and downstream performance gain, which offers a practical heuristic for selecting unpaired corpora.

Clear, well-structured paper with thorough ablations analyzing the choice of linear teacher (CCA, Procrustes, contrastive), divergences (CKA, InfoNCE, KLOT), and scaling behavior w.r.t. paired and unpaired sample counts.
weaknesses: Notational inconsistency in the gradient derivation: Equation (13) in Theorem 5.1 displays $\epsilon^*$ in the denominator, whereas Theorem C.4 in the Appendix correctly divides by $\epsilon$ (the entropic regularization parameter associated with the parameterized affinity matrix $K$).

Reliance on large batch sizes (up to 32k): although the explicit gradient avoids backpropagation through Sinkhorn iterations, computing Sinkhorn plans on large matrices at each training step still demands notable GPU memory and computation, and the sensitivity to smaller batch sizes is not fully characterized.

The alignment heads are restricted to linear mappings in the main benchmark; while linear projections are motivated by robustness against overfitting in low-supervision regimes, further exploration of expressive non-linear architectures (e.g., MLPs or lightweight adapters) would provide clearer guidance on model capacity trade-offs.

Empirical validation is limited to vision and language modalities; demonstrating applicability to domains where paired data is naturally much scarcer (e.g., audio, molecular/protein representations, or medical imaging modalities) would further strengthen the general claims.

strengths: Compelling formulation of a practical and under-explored problem: semi-supervised alignment of frozen unimodal representations in low-resource regimes where paired data are scarce but unpaired data are abundant.

A clean and elegant theoretical contribution (Theorem 5.1 / Theorem C.4): the authors derive an explicit closed-form expression for the gradient of the KLOT divergence, circumventing memory-heavy Sinkhorn unrolling and computationally slow implicit differentiation.

Extensive and rigorous experimental validation across multiple benchmarks, zero-shot classification, image-text retrieval, domain transfer (SkyScript satellite imagery), and cross-modality transfer (LibriSpeech speech-to-text).

Insightful diagnostic analyses, specifically demonstrating that mutual k-NN between frozen unimodal representations strongly correlates with alignability (Pearson r = 0.95), and showing that Spherical Sliced Wasserstein (SSW) distance effectively predicts performance under distribution shift.

Well-executed ablation and robustness studies, verifying resilience to teacher noise, dataset distribution shifts, and hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., entropic regularization ratio and loss weight).
weaknesses: Although the explicit gradient formula bypasses the memory overhead of unrolling Sinkhorn, the forward computation of entropic optimal transport still incurs quadratic $O(n^2)$ time complexity in batch size, which could present computational challenges if scaling to even larger batches.

The evaluation focuses exclusively on learning lightweight linear/shallow projection layers on top of frozen encoders; exploring whether the proposed KLOT regularization remains effective or stable when partially finetuning the underlying encoders would strengthen the scope.

Several semi-supervised baselines (such as NNCLR and S-CLIP) were adapted from domain adaptation or pretraining paradigms and required re-purposing for this specific unpaired-to-unpaired setup, meaning some baselines may not be as inherently well-suited to this exact formulation.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: aligning frozen unimodal encoders in low-supervision regimes where paired data is scarce but unpaired unimodal data is abundant.

Derives a clean, closed-form expression for the gradient of the optimal-transport-based KL divergence (Theorem 5.1 / C.4), circumventing the memory explosion of Sinkhorn unrolling and the computational overhead of implicit differentiation, thereby enabling efficient scaling to large batch sizes (up to 32k).

Thorough and comprehensive empirical validation across zero-shot image-text retrieval (COCO, Flickr30k), zero-shot classification (ImageNet and fine-grained benchmarks), satellite remote sensing (SkyScript), and cross-modal audio-text retrieval (LibriSpeech).

Extensive analysis of data dynamics, including robustness to teacher label noise, regularization hyperparameter sensitivity, encoder compatibility via mutual k-NN, and a quantitative analysis linking domain shift (Spherical Sliced Wasserstein distance) to downstream alignment performance.
weaknesses: The paper would benefit from greater clarity in the main text regarding the exact parameterization of the student alignment layers $f$ and $g$. Appendix A.1 reveals that $f$ and $g$ are linear projections ($d=1024$). Given that the teacher is also linear (e.g., CCA achieving 21.5 MeanR@1), the substantial boost of the student to 30.3 MeanR@1 via unpaired data regularization is a striking finding that warrants explicit emphasis and intuitive discussion in Section 3 or Section 6.1.

The theoretical novelty of the gradient in Theorem 5.1 should be contextualized more carefully relative to existing literature; the authors cite a blog post (Assel, 2024) and connections to the Monge Gap (Uscidda & Cuturi, 2023), so delineating what is new versus an application of known envelope theorem / entropic OT duality would strengthen the paper's scholarly framing.
A minor presentation omission: the code repository link is empty in the abstract ('Code is available at').

strengths: Compelling and practically important problem setting: Addressing vision-language (and multimodal) alignment when paired data is scarce (e.g., 1k-10k pairs) but unpaired unimodal data is abundant, connecting well with the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.

Theoretical and computational contribution in Theorem 5.1: The derivation of the closed-form gradient for the KLOT divergence avoids unrolling Sinkhorn iterations or computing expensive implicit differentiation, allowing scaling to large batch sizes (up to 32k) with dramatic memory and runtime reductions.

Thorough and strong empirical validation: SOTAlign consistently outperforms supervised baselines (SAIL, STRUCTURE) and adapted semi-supervised approaches (S-CLIP, NNCLR, SUE) across zero-shot retrieval (COCO, Flickr30k) and zero-shot classification (ImageNet, CIFAR, DTD, Food-101), achieving the same performance as SAIL with roughly 4x less supervision.

Broad generalization and insightful diagnostics: The authors validate the method beyond standard vision-language corpora to remote sensing (SkyScript) and speech-text (LibriSpeech), characterize distribution shifts using Spherical Sliced Wasserstein distance, and introduce mutual k-NN as an effective pre-training diagnostic tool.
weaknesses: Reliance on initial linear teacher quality: The second-stage pseudo-labeling/regularization is intrinsically bounded by the initial linear teacher. As shown in Figure 5, under extremely scarce supervision regimes (e.g., ~100 pairs), the linear model fails to establish a viable reference geometry, causing SOTAlign to collapse.

Incremental theoretical novelty of Theorem 5.1: While the application to large-batch cross-modal alignment is highly practical and well-executed, the mathematical result relies directly on established duality results and envelope theorem properties in entropic optimal transport (as acknowledged via connections to Monge Gap / Cuturi / Assel).

Scope limited to frozen unimodal encoders: The study strictly investigates training lightweight alignment heads atop frozen encoders. While well-motivated by the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and computationally economical, it remains unstudied whether or how this framework generalizes when encoders are partially or fully fine-tuned.
